list.listitem: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is rarely life-threatening and is an uncommon primary cause of hospitalization; an exception is SVT manifesting as a pre-excitation syndrome in sudden cardiac death (low incidence of 0.15%-0.39%). B
Intravenous adenosine or calcium-channel blockers are equally efficacious first-line agents for termination of acute episodes of SVT. A
Chronic prophylactic drug therapy or radiofrequency (RF) catheter ablation are the two options for treatment of patients with sustained/recurrent episodes of SVT. B
RF ablation of recurrent, highly symptomatic tachycardias is associated with more symptom relief, enhanced quality of life, and cost-effectiveness as compared to chronic drug therapy. B

background.definition: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is a narrow complex tachyarrhythmia with origination at or above the bundle of His. SVT episodes require atrial and/or atrioventricular nodal tissue for their initiation and maintenance of the tachyarrhythmia. Rhythms originate in these tissues and transmit through the bundle of His to the ventricles and cause a rapid ventricular response. SVTs can be classified based on the location of the reentry circuit, most often the atrioventricular nodal reentry tachycardia (AVNRT), atrioventricular reentry tachycardia (AVRT), or atrial tachycardia.

list.listitem: 35/100,000 person-years or 89,000 new cases are diagnosed each year.

In 1,754 patients undergoing catheter ablation for PSVTs, mean age was 45 +/- 19 years (range 5-96) and 62% of the cases were women. Another study found the mean age of symptom onset was 32±18 years of age for AVNRT, versus 23±14 years of age for AVRT.
Women are two times more likely than men to experience atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia, but accessory-pathway-mediated atrial arrhythmias are less common in women.
Those with "lone" PSVT are younger, have faster heart rates on presentation, and have more emergency room visits.
Prevalence is estimated at 2.25/1000 or 570,000 persons with PSVT in the United States.
PSVT is a frequent cause of emergency room and primary care physician visits, but is infrequently the primary reason for hospital admission.
SVT, especially in the young, is usually not associated with structural heart disease. Cardiac comorbidities are more common in patients over 50 years of age with SVTs.

Uncommon cardiac causes of SVT include congenital/structural heart disease (25% incidence of accessory pathways), myocardial scarring such as sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, prior atrial surgeries, primary electrical disorders such as long QT syndrome, and accessory pathways/familial pre-excitation.

Noncardiac causes that can induce reentry tachycardias include hyperthyroidism, electrolyte disturbances, drugs (stimulants, antibiotics, appetite suppressants, antiarrhythmics), and excessive intake of caffeine, alcohol, or recreational drugs.
Underlying mechanisms may be either abnormal impulse initiation (automaticity) or abnormal impulse conduction (reentry phenomenon). The latter mechanism is more common with SVT.
AVNRT uses a fast and slow pathways in the atrioventricular node for reentry and is the most common SVT (65%).
AVRT uses an accessory pathway that directly connects the atria and ventricles bypassing the AV node (30%).
Atrial tachycardia has a focal origin (5-10%).
Rare forms include sinus-node reentrant tachycardia, inappropriate sinus tachycardia, and junctional tachycardia.
Implantable loop recorders (ILR) are useful in the diagnosis of arrhythmias in patients with unexplained syncope with negative electrophysiologic and neurologic workup. B
Presence of pre-excitation on the ECG or a history of palpitations associated with syncope are indications for referral to an arrhythmia specialist for further electrophysiological workup. A

Differential.Differential_Features: Abrupt onset and termination of symptoms, pre-excitation common in AVRT
Abrupt onset and sometimes persistence of symptoms, presence of coexisting heart disease common, ECG findings of regular or irregular atrial tachycardia
More common in pulmonary, coronary, or valvular disease. ECG findings with irregular rhythm.
Progressive onset and termination of symptoms, normal ECG
Abrupt onset and termination of symptoms, syncope, wide/pathological Q waves

list.listitem: SVT has a heterogeneous clinical presentation. Symptoms described may include palpitations, fatigue, light-headedness, chest discomfort, dyspnea, presyncope, or syncope (15% of patients with SVT). Syncope may indicate concomitant structural abnormalities, such as valvular aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or cerebrovascular disease.

Symptoms vary with the ventricular rate, underlying heart disease, duration of SVT, and individual patient perceptions. Patients may describe the pattern in terms of the number of episodes, duration, frequency, mode of onset, and possible triggers.
Acute presentations can include angina, decompensated heart failure, pulmonary edema, and hypotension.
PSVT has abrupt onset and termination. Patients with PSVT are most often asymptomatic, especially in the young with no underlying structural heart disease.
Termination of symptoms/arrhythmia by vagal maneuvers suggests a reentrant tachycardia involving the AV node.
Patients with suspected arrhythmia should have a 12-lead ECG taken during the arrhythmia with SVT having a narrow QRS complex (<120 milliseconds) unless there is aberrant atrioventricular conduction.

Ambulatory 24 or 48-hour Holter monitoring can be used in patients with frequent but transient arrhythmias. For those who have events less frequently, a 14 or 21-day adhesive patch monitor or an event/implantable loop recorder may be more useful.
Electrophysiological evaluation is indicated in the presence of pre-excitation (Wolf-Parkinson-White syndrome) on the resting ECG.
Echocardiogram should be considered with sustained SVT to rule out underlying structural heart disease.
Consider electrolyte and thyroid function testing; however, these appear to have a low yield.
With a sensitivity and specificity of >96%, the Brugada criteria can help distinguish between SVT with aberrancy and ventricular tachycardia.
A study of 124 patients with SVT found that elevated troponin was not associated with an increase in the 5 year risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, so it should be interpreted cautiously.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation of the patient with SVT.
Intravenous adenosine or calcium-channel blockers are equally effective first-line agents for termination of acute episodes of SVTs. A
Chronic prophylactic drug therapy and RF ablation are the two options for treatment of patients with sustained/recurrent episodes of SVT. B
RF ablation of the nodal pathway in AV-nodal reentrant tachycardia has been associated with a high success rate (95% in one study). B
RF ablation of recurrent, highly symptomatic tachycardias is associated with more symptom relief, enhanced quality of life, and cost-effectiveness as compared to chronic drug therapy. B
Acute and chronic management of SVTs should be initiated based on the identified underlying mechanism (i.e., automaticity vs reentry phenomenon).

Initial management of the arrhythmia depends on the hemodynamic status of the patient. Any hemodynamically unstable narrow or wide QRS-complex tachycardia should be terminated with synchronized direct current cardioversion.
See for acute management of patients with hemodynamically stable and regular tachycardias. All treatment is initiated with continuous ECG monitoring and monitoring of vital signs.

Vagal maneuvers are thought to be useful in tachycardias involving the atrioventricular node, although the evidence in controlled clinical trials is lacking. These include Valsalva (blowing into a mouthpiece with sustained resistance for at least 30 seconds), unilateral carotid massage after exclusion of a carotid bruit with head tilted to the other side and not exceeding 10 seconds, and facial immersion in cold water. They are most effective when performed shortly after onset of the arrhythmia and have a success rate of about 25%. The modified Valsalva maneuver is more effective than the standard Valsalva maneuver. In the modified Valsalva, patients perform a standardized strain in a semirecumbent position, then immediately lay flat and have their legs raised to 45 degrees for 15 seconds, and then return to a semirecumbent position. It reduces anti-arrhythmic use without increasing time in the ED or adverse events. Valsalva is more effective in adults and facial immersion or application of ice pack to the face in infants.

Though adenosine is consider first-line, randomized controlled trials have shown similar efficacy for adenosine and calcium-channel blockers.A 2012 meta-analysis found the conversion rate for adenosine and verapamil was 90.8% (95% CI: 87.3-93.4%) and 89.9% (95% CI: 86.0-92.9%), respectively. Intravenous diltiazem is similar to intravenous verapamil for AVNRT.

A retrospective cohort study of 212 ED patients presenting with SVT found a higher initial termination rate with return to sinus rhythm with 12 mg as opposed to 6 mg of adenosing (79.1% vs 56.4%) and no difference in adverse events.

The advantage of adenosine over calcium-channel blockers and beta blockers relates to its rapid onset of action (within 30 seconds) and short half-life (less than 10 seconds). It works by inhibiting conduction through the AV node and is given by a rapid peripheral intravenous push of 6 mg to 12 mg followed by a 10 to 30 mL saline flush. Increasing doses of 12 to 18 mg may be repeated twice. Administration via a central line requires dose reduction (1 mg). Contraindications include wide QRS-complex tachycardia, severe coronary artery disease, heart transplant patients, and severe bronchial asthma. When administered in patients with pre-excitation syndrome, it can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation.

A Chinese study randomized 122 patients with paroxysmal SVT to IV adenosine, modified Valsalva maneuver, and combined treatment. Rates of success were 42% for Valsalva, 75% for adenosine and 86% for the combination, although the difference between adenosing and combined therapy was not statistically significant.

Longer acting AV-nodal blocking agents such as calcium-channel blockers and beta blockers are useful in patients with recurrent premature atrial or ventricular beats. Verapamil is given in doses of 5 to 10 mg intravenously over 2 to 3 minutes and repeated every 3 to 5 minutes to a maximum of 15 mg if necessary. Metoprolol is given as a 5 mg intravenous bolus and repeated in 5 minutes times two if necessary.
A small randomized, crossover study found intravenous diltiazem to be superior to esmolol in terminating SVT (p < 0.001).
Extreme caution is necessary with concomitant use of intravenous beta blockers and calcium-channel blockers, as this can cause significant bradycardia and hypotension.
AV-nodal blocking agents should be avoided in patients with wide QRS-complex tachycardias unless there is strong evidence that it is AV-node dependent.
If the specific diagnosis of a wide QRS-complex tachycardia cannot be made, it should be treated as ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise.

Episodic treatment of infrequent, well-tolerated PSVT using a "pill-in-the-pocket" approach with either single-dose oral flecainide (3 mg/kg) or a combination of diltiazem (120 mg) and propranolol (80 mg) may minimize the need for emergency room visits by these patients.
Patients should be educated on how to perform vagal maneuvers.
Chronic prophylactic drug therapy is indicated for patients with sustained/recurrent episodes of SVT.
AV-node dependent SVT may be treated with high doses of calcium-channel blockers (480 mg/day of verapamil), beta-adrenergic blockers (240 mg/day of propranolol), or digoxin (0.375 mg/day).

Class IC agents like flecainide (200-300 mg/day) and propafenone (300 mg three times daily) affect both the AV-node and accessory pathways and reduce episode frequency. They are contraindicated in patients with structural heart disease. Concomitant therapy with beta-adrenergic blockers enhance efficacy.
Flecainide has been shown to be more effective than verapamil in suppressing recurrences of SVT, with a greater percentage achieving complete remission (30% vs 13%, p = 0.03, NNT = 6).

A single randomized controlled study showed that propafenone reduced the recurrence rate of PSVT more than placebo (relative risk of recurrence with placebo = 6.8). Doses higher than 300 mg were associated with more adverse effects.
Class III agents such as sotalol, dofetilide, and amiodarone are second-line agents. Amiodarone has been shown to be safe in patients with structural heart disease.

RF ablation is indicated in patients with pre-excitation syndromes such as AVRT and AVNRT and focal atrial tachycardia in patients who desire to avoid or are intolerant or unresponsive to drug therapy.

Because of drug efficacy rates of 30% to 50%, it may be offered as first-line therapy to patients with recurrent tachycardia. The decision to ablate instead of using drug therapy is often patient-specific, and is related to lifestyle issues, patient preference, and the availability of an experienced center for ablation. See .

RF ablation of the nodal pathway in AVNRT has a high success rate.A meta-analysis of 39 studies found a single procedure success rate of 93.2% and a multiple procedure success rate of 94.6%; postablation arrhythmias occurred in 5.6% of patients, adverse events were seen in 0.5%, and all-cause mortality was 0.6%. There is low-risk of AV-nodal block and requirement for pacemaker implantation with RF ablation.
Patients with well-tolerated episodes of PSVT that either terminate spontaneously or respond to vagal maneuvers do not require chronic prophylactic therapy.
Chronic prophylactic drug therapy is indicated for patients with sustained/recurrent episodes of SVT.

Conditions warranting referral to an electrophysiologist include tachycardia with a wide QRS complex, SVT with syncope or severe symptoms, a patient with drug resistance or intolerance or with a preference to be free of drug therapy, and manifestation of a pre-excitation syndrome (with or without SVT).
SVTs are rarely life-threatening and are an uncommon primary cause of hospitalization; an exception is SVT manifestation as a pre-excitation syndrome in sudden cardiac death. B

SVTs are rarely life-threatening and are an uncommon primary cause of hospitalization; an exception is SVT manifestation as a pre-excitation syndrome in sudden cardiac death (low incidence of 0.15%-0.39%).
Untreated sustained tachyarrhythmias will, in course of time, lead to cardiomyopathy and congestive heart failure.
Remission rate for chronic drug therapy for SVT is 30% to 50%; it can be as high as 95% for RF ablation.
RF ablation reduces the recurrence of the arrhythmia and the need for rehospitalization, and improves quality of life.
RF ablation of SVT in patients who have associated atrial fibrillation also reduces the recurrence of idiopathic atrial fibrillation in these patients.
Surgical repair of congenital heart conditions that involve atrial incisions predispose to incision-related atrial flutter late after surgery.
Calcium-channel blockers and beta blockers are effective in reducing postoperative atrial tachyarrhythmia. Beta blockers, however, tend to increase the risk of pulmonary edema.

Using dexmedetomidine for sedation during electrophysiology studies and ablation was not associated with a reduction in PSVT inducibility in a retrospective review but was associated with an increased incidence of intraprocedure hypotension.
Patients should be advised to avoid relevant risk factors such as caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol.
Comorbid conditions and congenital heart disorders should be treated appropriately.
About 20% of those with a history of PSVT will have symptomatic exacerbation during pregnancy.
RF ablation should be recommended in women with symptomatic and recurrent tachycardias before they contemplate pregnancy. If needed during pregnancy, it should be avoided in the 1st trimester.

Acute management of symptomatic SVT may be done using vagal maneuvers, adenosine, and beta blockers. Verapamil may be associated with a greater risk of maternal hypotension and fetal hypoperfusion. DC cardioversion is safe in all phases of pregnancy.
If prophylactic drug therapy is needed, digoxin or a beta blocker is the first-line agent. Avoid beta blockers, if possible, during the first trimester.
All currently available antiarrhythmic drugs are classified Class C during pregnancy except sotalol (Class B) and atenolol and amiodarone (Class D).
Use of antiarrhythmics during the first trimester may be associated with increased risk of teratogenicity and during later trimesters with adverse effects on fetal growth and development.
SVT is the most common cause of fetal tachyarrhythmia (73.2%), and is associated with hydrops fetalis in 40% and a mortality rate of 8.9%.
Clinical presentation varies with the age. SVT can present as congestive heart failure in the newborn and infancy period and as palpitations and dizziness during childhood and adolescence.
For non-pharmacologic interventions, the use of facial immersion or application of ice pack to the face is more successful in infants than carotid massage.
Adenosine is the drug of choice in any age group for termination of atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia.
Pharmacologic treatment of SVT is preferable in newborn babies and infants due to the high spontaneous cessation rate at the end of the first year of life.
In children >1 year of age, due to the low spontaneous remission rate, RF ablation is a rational alternative to long-term pharmacological therapy.

Ambulatory adhesive monitoring for up to two weeks can be helpful for those with infrequent episodes. In a national registry study of >3000 children, 44% of first-detected arrythmias occured after 48 hours.
